book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook starts from purchasing power parity (absolute PPP, then relative PPP: the inflation differential predicts depreciation) and then mentions the law of one price and its frictions. The video goes the other way: it runs one good through two concrete what-if cases on one scene (price gap -> trade -> currency demand -> new rate), answers the learner's doubt about the payment currency, generalises the two cases into the inflation rule, turns the rule into an exam-style table, only then admits the frictions with a real-life price (₹110, not ₹160), and finally widens the one good into a basket to compute the PPP rate. The term PPP comes last, as the name for something already calculated.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: One object, many cases: each piece changes one price on the same two-country scene and follows the money until the rate settles; the cases are then generalised into a rule, and the single object is widened into a basket to define the formal measure.

moves.concept: general rule: inflation -> depreciation

moves.concept: general rule: inflation -> depreciation

moves.concept: inflation differential and the exchange rate (>, <, =); devaluation -> inflation

moves.concept: inflation differential and the exchange rate (>, <, =); devaluation -> inflation

moves.concept: inflation differential and the exchange rate (>, <, =); devaluation -> inflation

narration.density: About 9 new ideas in 6 minutes (depreciation to equilibrium, payment-currency neutrality, inflation, inflation differential, devaluation -> inflation, frictions, standard basket, PPP rate, market vs PPP), about 1.5 per minute at about 193 words per minute. The two long cases (2 minutes) give the core mechanism room; the devaluation-inflation link and the PPP-market link at the end are rushed.

talmel_summary: Strong fit: most tiles land together (16 of 24), and in the two cases every spoken step has its own drawn step (price struck, truck route, payment loop, demand tag, rate struck), including the learner's objection, where the rupee loop dissolves on 'rupees mein nahi'. The best single sync is the forex counter vanishing on 'bhool jaayein'. Weak: the new rates (80, 20) appear on 'depreciate' about 5 s before their numbers are spoken; the inflation-differential rule and the frictions are text the voice reads out; and 14 s of speech (254.5-268.1 s) is missing from the transcript.

voice.notes: About 193 words per minute, quick but clear, with 'soch ke dekhiye' and 'abvious si baat hai' marking each turn of a case. Numbers are read in mixed Hindi-English ('1 dollar is equal to 80 rupees', '4000 divided by 100'); the recogniser sometimes writes '$80' for '80 rupees'. The objection is voiced in a natural second-person tone ('aap kahoge'), and the exam question is put to the listener directly. Little pausing between ideas in the last two minutes.

game_ideas.player_does: Sets the chocolate's price in India and in the US with two sliders, predicts where the rupee-dollar rate will settle, then releases the traders.
game_ideas.process_happens: Trucks start running from the cheaper country to the dearer one; each delivery sends a payment to the forex counter, the demand tag for the paying currency grows and the rate pill ticks until the two prices match at the new rate; then the trucks stop.
game_ideas.win: The predicted rate is within 5% of where the trucks stop (for example ₹160 / $2 -> 80; ₹160 / $8 -> 20).
game_ideas.lose: A wrong prediction leaves trucks running and the profit gap visible on both price tags, showing the rate has not yet settled.
game_ideas.concept: case 1: home prices rise -> imports -> dollar demand -> rupee depreciates

game_ideas.player_does: Gets a pair of countries with yearly inflation rates (for example US 3%, India 6%) and drags an arrow on the rate pill to say which currency weakens, or marks it stable.
game_ideas.process_happens: A year passes: price tags in each panel rise by their inflation, trucks run toward the dearer country's buyers, and the rate pill moves accordingly.
game_ideas.win: The right direction for the >, < and = cases, three rounds in a row.
game_ideas.lose: A wrong direction makes the trucks run against the player's arrow and the price tags show the gap that drives them.
game_ideas.concept: inflation differential and the exchange rate (>, <, =); devaluation -> inflation

game_ideas.player_does: Fills the same basket in both countries (rice, bus fare, haircut, mobile recharge) from a dollar price list and a rupee price list, then divides to get the PPP rate and compares it with the market rate pill.
game_ideas.process_happens: Basket totals appear over each basket, the forex counter fades out while a band joins the baskets, the division animates and a PPP pill appears beside the market pill.
game_ideas.win: The correct PPP rate and the correct statement of which currency buys more at home than its market rate suggests.
game_ideas.lose: Putting different items in the two baskets gives a wrong rate and the band flashes 'not the same basket'.
game_ideas.concept: PPP exchange rate from a standard basket

checks_learned: When a rate or price changes, the new number should land on its spoken number, not on the general verb ('depreciate'); here 80 and 20 appear about 5 s early.
A mirrored case that starts from the previous case's end state must say so ('ab rate 80 hai'); otherwise a learner computes from the original state and gets the wrong rate.
Every number set in a worked case must satisfy the rule it shows: home price / foreign price = new rate (160/2 = 80, 160/8 = 20, 4000/100 = 40 all pass here); this can be a code check.
An objection voiced by the narrator ('aap kahoge') should change the picture (erase the old path, draw the new one); it worked here and can be required.
A rule given as a text table (>, <, =) should be followed by one animated case per row, reusing the scene already built.
Market rules stated as certain ('tay hai') need a qualifier (relative to the partner country, other things equal) or a flag.
No branded product as a running object; draw a generic one.
Transcript gaps over 10 s (254.5-268.1 s here) must be re-transcribed; the spoken list of frictions was lost.

teaching_best.why: a what-if on a single price drives a full cause chain on one scene, each link drawn as it is said
the learner's objection about the payment currency is voiced and answered on the picture, removing a doubt most learners would have
two worked cases are generalised into a rule, and the term inflation is attached only after the learner has seen it work twice
the rule is turned into an exam-style question with a short model answer
'forget the market rate for a moment': PPP is computed with the market removed, then named

teaching_weak.why: says 'the reverse' but starts from case 1's end numbers (1$ = 80, ₹160) without saying so
devaluation -> inflation is added in one sentence with no case or numbers
the list of frictions is lost from the transcript and lives on screen as a paragraph
the claimed link between the PPP rate and the market rate is unexplained and doubtful as stated
the rule is stated as certain for any rise in prices; it holds for inflation relative to the partner country
